Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a **high‑level playbook** – written as if I were a software agent equipped only with 1️⃣ “search‑internet” → returns URLs / snippets describing public RESTful interfaces, and 2️⃣ “execute‑api-call(string)” → takes a fully‑formed HTTP request expressed as a single string (method + URL + headers + body) and runs it against the target service. I’ll walk through each phase, showing concrete examples where possible, while keeping in mind that many commercial chains such as McDonald’s do *not* expose open “order‑food” APIs to the public. In practice you’d often hit a private internal API behind their own web/mobile app, which requires OAuth credentials, device IDs, and sometimes even signed JWTs. For illustration, let’s assume there exists a publicly documented endpoint `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order`. --- ### Phase 1 – Discover the Ordering Endpoint | Step | What to Do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | 1. Call the search tool | `"find McDonalds online ordering api"` | Pull all references to official or unofficial APIs. | | 2. Inspect results | Look for links pointing at `/docs`, `/swagger.json`, or GitHub repos titled “McD Order SDK”. | These usually contain the exact paths, required query params, and sample payloads. | | 3. Verify authenticity | Check domain ownership (`mcdonalds.com`), presence of HTTPS, and whether the documentation mentions “public API” vs “internal.” | Avoid phishing or malicious services. | > **Result:** Suppose we locate a Swagger spec at `https://api.mcdonalds.com/docs/swagger.yaml`. It shows: > > ``` > POST /v1/orders > - Header: Authorization: Bearer > - Body: { > "items": [ > { "sku": "BURGER_001", "qty": 1 }, > { "sku": "FRIES_SMALL", "qty": 1 } > ], > "payment_method_id": "", > "delivery_address": "...", > ... > } > ``` If no public doc appears, you might have to reverse‑engineer the mobile/web front‑end using network sniffers—outside the scope here. --- ### Phase 2 – Authenticate & Acquire Tokens Most modern e‑commerce APIs demand some sort of bearer token. Typical flows: | Flow | Steps | Example Request | |------|-------|-----------------| | **OAuth2 Client Credentials** | 1. Get `client_id/client_secret` from dev portal.
2. POST to `https://api.mcdonalds.com/oauth/token` with grant_type=client_credentials.|``POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/oauth/token\nHeaders:\n Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded\nBody:\n grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=&client_secret=`| | **API Key** | Include `x-api-key:` header on every request. |``GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu\nHeader: x-api-key: ABC123XYZ```| Assume we’ve obtained a valid access token `eyJhbGciOiJIUz...`. --- ### Phase 3 – Build the Order Payload From the swagger snippet we saw the minimal fields: ```json { "items": [ { "sku": "BURGER_001", "qty": 1 }, { "sku": "FRIES_SMALL", "qty": 1 } ], "payment_method_id": "card_last4_4242", "delivery_address": { "street": "1600 Amphitheatre Parkway", "city": "Mountain View", "state": "CA", "zip": "94043" }, "instructions": "Please ring the bell." } ``` In plain text suitable for our executor: ``` POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUz... Content-Type: application/json { "items":[{"sku":"BURGER_001","qty":1},{"sku":"FRIES_SMALL","qty":1}], "payment_method_id":"card_last4_4242", "delivery_address":{"street":"1600 Amphitheatre Pkwy","city":"Mountain View","state":"CA","zip":"94043"}, "instructions":"Ring the bell!" } ``` *(Note: Replace placeholders with your real address/payment details.)* --- ### Phase 4 – Execute the Call Using the “string‑form” executor: ```python response = execute_api_call(""" POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUz... Content-Type: application/json { ...payload json... } """) print(response.status_code) print(response.body) ``` Typical responses: | Status Code | Meaning | Sample Body | |-------------|---------|--------------| | 201 Created | Order accepted | `{ "orderId": "abc123", "estimatedDeliveryTime": "12:34 PM" }` | | 400 Bad Request | Missing/invalid SKU | `{ "error": "SKU BURGER_001 unknown." }` | | 401 Unauthorized | Token expired | `{ "error": "Invalid token." }` | Handle errors accordingly: refresh token, retry after delay, or fall back to manual ordering. --- ### Phase 5 – Post‑Order Actions Once you receive a successful response: 1. Store the returned `orderId`. 2. Optionally poll status endpoint: `GET /v1/orders/{orderId}` until state changes to `delivered` or `cancelled`. 3. Notify the customer (e.g., push notification, email). Example polling loop (pseudo): ```text while True: resp = execute_api_call(f""" GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders/{orderId} Authorization: Bearer """) status = resp.body["status"] if status == "completed": notify_user("Your burger and fries are ready!") break elif status == "failed": alert_admin(...) break sleep(30) ``` --- ### Caveats & Practical Tips | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|-----------| | **No Public API** | Reverse engineer the mobile app’s traffic (Wireshark/Fiddler); look for hidden endpoints. | | **Rate Limits** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; implement exponential backoff. | | **Payment Security** | Never store raw card numbers; rely on PCI‑compliant payment gateway tokens. | | **Legal Compliance** | Ensure you’re authorized to use the API; read terms-of-service. | | **Testing Environment** | Many vendors provide sandbox/test keys; never test live payments unless absolutely necessary. | --- #### Bottom Line With just a “search‑for‑APIs” tool and an “execute‑request-as-string” tool, the workflow boils down to: 1. Find the correct endpoint and schema. 2. Obtain authorization (bearer token/API key). 3. Craft the JSON payload for burger + fries. 4. Send the request and handle the response. That’s essentially what a backend microservice would do under the hood when placing an automated order for you!
